the American edition], 1803); E. Claude Savary, Letters on Egypt (English trans., 2 vols, 1787);
Count Volney, Travels through Syria and Egypt . . . (English trans., 2 vols, 1793); and a number
of other works, including Raleigh’s History of the World, James Bruce’s Travels to Discover the
Source of the Nile (5 vols, 1790), and Robert Walpole’s Memoirs (1817). In short, the account in
Diodorus Siculus had filtered by many routes into the general literary culture in which S. was
steeped, and he was undoubtedly familiar with the figure of Ozymandias and his remnants.
